newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan business leaders oppose five-day work week.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan business leaders oppose five-day work week.

text.p: Taiwan's business leaders on Wednesday attacked a government decision to begin a five-day work week from 1998, saying the move would hurt the island's competitiveness.
"When the per capita income reaches US$20,000, local industries will adopt a five-day work week," Wang You-tseng, chairman of the General Chamber of Commerce, told reporters.
"At the time when we are trying to increase our competitiveness, implementing the five-day work week will be detrimental," Wang added.
Taiwan's per capita income stood at some US$12,000.
Taiwan's cabinet on Tuesday approved a proposal to begin a five-day work week, giving public servants two days off every second and fourth week of each month effective from January 1998.

"The programme was approved under the condition that the public would not receive less quality service from public servants," an official quoted government spokesman David Lee as telling reporters on Tuesday.
The private sector will not be forced to follow suit, but will have the option of doing so, the official said.
When asked whether he would follow the new system, Kao Chin-yen, chairman of the Chinese National Federation of Industries and chairman of food giant President Enterprises, said: "Not now."
Public servants and many private sector employees now have to work four hours on Saturdays.
Officials said the new policy would not reduce government agencies' work hours because public servants would no longer have days off from eight national holidays.

Taiwan's stock, bond, money and foreign exchange markets would follow the programme to close on every second and fourth Saturday of the month, but open on the said eight national holidays, officials said.
Officials declined to give a timetable for implementing an overall five-day work week.
